drills.q: State Aurora's replication factor and quorum numbers for reads and writes.
drills.a: 6 copies across 3 AZs (2 per AZ). Writes need a 4-of-6 quorum, reads need a 3-of-6 quorum. 4+3>6 guarantees overlap between any read and write quorum.

drills.q: Why is Aurora failover faster than standard RDS Multi-AZ failover, mechanically?
drills.a: Aurora replicas already share the writer's distributed storage layer, so failover is just promoting a reader's role -- no separate standby storage to catch up or rebuild. Standard RDS Multi-AZ promotes a synchronously-replicated standby with its own separate storage volume and redirects DNS, which takes longer (1-2 min vs Aurora's typically under 60s).

drills.q: A DynamoDB table throttles on specific items while CloudWatch shows consumed capacity well under the provisioned total. Diagnose and explain why adding more table-wide capacity won't fix it.
drills.a: A hot partition -- one partition is hitting its hard ceiling of 3,000 RCU/1,000 WCU per second regardless of the table's overall headroom. Adding table-wide capacity doesn't raise any individual partition's ceiling; the fix is redesigning the partition key for better distribution (random/hashed suffix, sharding the hot key).

drills.q: Is single-table DynamoDB design a best practice to recommend by default? Justify.
drills.a: No. It's a deliberate tradeoff for high-scale, access-pattern-stable workloads with real DynamoDB expertise on the team. For most teams, multi-table design is easier to reason about and evolve as access patterns change -- even the pattern's original advocate has publicly acknowledged the backlash against applying it as a default.

drills.q: Why would you choose a GSI over an LSI for a new secondary access pattern you're not fully certain about yet?
drills.a: LSIs can only be defined at table creation time and can never be added or removed afterward, while GSIs can be added, modified, or removed anytime with automatic backfill. Unless you specifically need an LSI's strongly-consistent-read capability, the flexibility of GSIs makes them the safer default for an uncertain future access pattern.

drills.q: How much more expensive is a DynamoDB TransactWriteItems call than an equivalent plain PutItem, and when do you actually need it?
drills.a: 2x the capacity units. Needed only when true cross-item or cross-table atomicity is required (all-or-nothing across multiple items); for single-item idempotency, a conditional write (ConditionExpression) provides the same safety at half the capacity cost.

drills.q: What changed with Aurora Serverless v2 in November 2024, and what's the tradeoff of the new capability?
drills.a: It gained scale-to-zero: a database with no active connections for a configurable idle period pauses entirely, billing only storage, and resumes in roughly 15 seconds on the next connection. The tradeoff is that 15-second cold-resume latency is visible to whatever makes the first request after an idle period -- fine for internal/dev workloads, likely unacceptable for a synchronous customer-facing path with continuous traffic.

drills.q: A team wants to migrate a MongoDB app to DocumentDB purely for cost. What specific compatibility gaps must be tested first?
drills.a: No retryable writes (app-level retry/error-handling must be added explicitly), no $graphLookup aggregation stage, and missing or limited support for capped collections, GridFS, text indexes, vector search indexes, and partial indexes, among others. CRUD and most indexing generally work unchanged, but every aggregation pipeline in actual use needs explicit testing against DocumentDB before committing to the migration.

drills.q: Why did ElastiCache shift its default engine recommendation to Valkey, and what does that mean for existing Redis OSS users?
drills.a: Redis's license changed to SSPL/RSALv2 in 2024 and gained an AGPLv3 option in 2025, moving it away from a permissive open-source license. Valkey is the Linux Foundation-governed BSD-licensed fork from Redis OSS 7.2 that ElastiCache now defaults to for new deployments. ElastiCache only carries legacy Redis OSS support up to version 7.2, so anyone wanting newer Redis-compatible features must move to Valkey.

drills.q: When is Neptune (or any graph database) the right architectural choice over a relational database with join tables?
drills.a: When the dominant query shape is deep, multi-hop traversal -- fraud-ring detection, recommendation collaborative filtering, social-graph queries -- where relational join cost grows with hop count but graph traversal cost per hop stays roughly constant. Wrong for workloads that are mostly single-entity lookups with shallow joins, where relational remains simpler and cheaper to operate.

drills.q: How did the November 2024 DynamoDB price cut change the on-demand vs provisioned decision, and what workload shape still favors provisioned?
drills.a: On-demand pricing dropped substantially, making it the recommended default for unpredictable or lower-volume workloads. Sustained, predictable throughput at realistic utilization (~70%+) still favors provisioned with auto-scaling, which remains commonly 3-4x cheaper at that utilization level, with the gap widening further near 100% utilization.
